newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaire exiles come out of shadows to back rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire exiles come out of shadows to back rebels.

text.p: Tutsi guerrillas battling Zairean troops in eastern Zaire won support on Wednesday from an unlikely location -- Zairean exiles gathered in a hotel opposite the train station in downtown Lausanne.

On a rainy day in Lausanne, in a rented corner of a hotel lobby, former Zairean army Colonel Felix Mbayi-Kalombo launched a new opposition group at a news conference and vowed to fight to topple Zaire's long-serving strongman Mobutu Sese Seko.

Mbayi-Kalombo, a U.S.-trained former Zairean army troop commander sacked by Mobutu in 1978, was adviser to Zaire's former reformist prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, a long-time Mobutu foe fired in 1992.
He fled Zaire in 1993 for exile in Switzerland after being imprisoned for four months by Mobutu, released and then shot in the leg by suspected security forces.

Flanked by burly Zairean supporters dressed in loud silk shirts and trenchcoats, Mbayi-Kalombo said his group would back Laurent Kabila, leader of Zaire's Tutsi rebels who have taken large swathes of east Zaire, in the struggle to topple Mobutu.
"If Kabila is fighting to rid Zaire of Mobutu, if he thinks like we do, we are prepared to work with him. We are ready to support him. The goal is one -- to fight the dictator," he said.
Mbayi-Kalombo was secretive about his new opposition group, the Re-assembly of the Fighting Forces of Zaire and it is unclear how much support he commands.
But the lightning Tutsi rebellion has provided a half-open door for other Zairean opposition groups nursing fierce hatred towards Mobutu to capitalise.
Western diplomats say many Zairean opposition groups large or small are expected to try to take advantage of the success of the Tutsi revolt to follow their own agendas.
Mbayi-Kalombo claimed he had support from officers in the Zairean army in capital Kinshasa as well as exiled former Zairean officers in Europe in his bid to topple Mobutu.
"Our aim is to fight Mobutu. Our weapon is the will of the Zairean people," he said. "We cannot tell you much now, but you will be hearing more and more from us."

Swiss waiters watched from a corner as the exiles whispered of secret preparations in Kinshasa for an army coup and made appeals for cash to topple Mobutu -- who was in Lausanne until recently for two-and-half months of cancer treatment.
Those who turned up at the press conference included "Lumumbists" -- followers of Zaire's first prime minister, leftist Patrice Lumumba who was assasinated in January 1961.

Rebel leader Kabila, 56, too takes his inspiration from Lumumba. A long-time opponent of Mobutu, he is a comrade-in-arms in the 1960s of Marxist guerrilla Che Guevara. Kabila, from mineral-rich southern Zaire, is not a Tutsi and has opposed Mobutu since a 1960s rebellion just after independence.

"We're not alone. We have many friends in Zaire. We'll fight Mobutu with all means. We'll take up arms since we have no other choice," Mbayi-Calombo said. "Our movement is not limited to the Tutsis of Zaire. We must unite to get rid of the dictator."
